title: Laptop Tech Support Showdown: Apple
description: Topping our tech support rankings for the third year in a row, Apple has the best combination of phone and web support. Read our full tech support review: http://www.laptopmag.com/articles/apple-tech-support

asr.full_text: . Not everyone loves Apple's new MacBooks and the MacBook Pros, but their tech support is still tops. According to our own survey, and Henry went undercover to test their tech support, why are they still number one? Experience above and beyond everybody else. It's friendly, fast. That is the big thing about getting tech support. You want to be out before you're even starting. Right. But also, it's a fun experience. You get to choose the kind of music you want to listen to. You just said fun and tech support. Yeah, right? What? Weird. So, what about, so when you called them, actually what was really cool is that they have Twitter now, which they didn't have before. So, what was the response like? Quick times on Twitter, I think it was a little bit under maybe 15 minutes, sometimes. When I Twitter, I think it was a little under 15 minutes. I actually wrote our first article on Apple Twitter text support. Back then, it was in minutes you would get a reply under 10. And now it's around 15, maybe 40, depending on what time of day. But every time, they give you a link to the answer and solves your query. Even if they could explain it in the tweet, you still have to click the link. But it explains what you need to know. So they're not on Facebook but pretty good on Twitter. Yeah, and not everybody does Facebook, but improvements are always there. When it comes to tech support over the phone, do you just call them? Or do you try to set up an appointment online and then do it that way? I would use their website to click to have them call me. And I think that's really better because it, first of all, you go through the phone tree in a way without even going to the phone tree, you have a button interface that says, oh this is my product, this is my issue and then they already know what's up, they already have your device mentioned when you already enter your account information. Right, what I liked about the way that you tested is that you asked them questions about new features, stuff that other brands might not really get. So, how did they do? Two out of three well, maybe two and a half out of three. Siri and the touch bar they aced. One of the things about Mac OS Sierra that some people might accidentally lock themselves into or walk into is Desktop Documents iCloud, which is where it mirrors yourself in the cloud and maybe you have too many items in your desktop or documents folder right you might want to undo that if you want to keep spending money on iCloud. When I asked them how to do that they sort of explained it but they could have done a better and more thorough job of answering it. But, activating Siri and getting the function keys back on the Touch Bar, they knew that instantaneously. Okay. So they're still number one, is there any advice that you would give to them if Apple was listening right now? As I said, make sure when macOS Sierra drops, or no, whatever macOS 10, 13 is gonna be this year. Right. Make sure the geniuses know what's new and how to use and undo what it introduces, but also Facebook exists, it's got a lot of users. Twitter's nice but nobody's sure how long it's gonna be for really. So maybe we don't invest all of our eggs in that social basket. So definitely branch out but overall if you want to see the results of every brand in the tech support showdown make sure you go to LaptopMag.com, this is Mark Spoon Alan.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as a Laptop Mag tech-support review about Apple, covering rankings, survey results, and an undercover support test. The described actions involve ordinary support and information-seeking, including using Apple’s website for a callback and discussing Siri, Touch Bar, and iCloud mirroring. The invitation to visit Tom’s Guide forums is an audience discussion prompt, not a payment request, investment offer, credential request, or deceptive benefit flow.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The central subject is an ordinary commercial technical-support service being reviewed and tested, including phone, web, callback, and Twitter support. The supplied evidence does not show a scam mechanism.
